questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of treating staff as an asset?
options: Treating employees as a valuable resource worth investing in because they add value
Treating employees as an expense to be minimised
Recording employees on the statement of financial position
Employing only permanent full-time staff
questions.why: The asset approach invests in training, pay and security, expecting a return through higher productivity, lower turnover and better service.
whyNot: That is the staff-as-a-cost approach, the opposite.
Employees are not recorded as assets in accounts. The phrase describes an attitude, not an accounting treatment.
Contract type is a separate question. A business can value its staff and still use some flexible contracts.

questions.stem: Which term is defined as: ending a person's employment because the job itself is no longer needed?
options: Redundancy
Dismissal
Resignation
Retirement
questions.why: Redundancy is about the job disappearing, not the person's performance, which is why compensation is normally payable and the role should not be refilled.
whyNot: Dismissal is about the person: their conduct or their capability.
Resignation is the employee choosing to leave.
Retirement is leaving work at the end of a career.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of a zero-hour contract?
options: A contract with no guaranteed minimum number of working hours
A contract with no pay for the first month
A contract that cannot be ended by either side
A contract for exactly zero hours of work
questions.why: The employer offers hours as needed and is not obliged to provide any. Maximum flexibility for the business, minimum security for the worker.
whyNot: Unpaid work is a separate matter and generally unlawful. Zero-hour refers to guaranteed hours, not to pay rates.
Zero-hour contracts are usually easier to end, not harder.
Hours are worked; they are simply not guaranteed in advance.

questions.stem: Which term is defined as: training employees to carry out more than one role so they can be moved between tasks?
options: Multi-skilling
Outsourcing
Delayering
Job rotation
questions.why: Multi-skilling is a form of workforce flexibility. It covers absence, reduces idle time and needs investment in training.
whyNot: Outsourcing pays another business to do work previously done in-house.
Delayering removes levels of hierarchy.
Job rotation moves an employee between tasks to reduce boredom. It is a motivation method; multi-skilling is about capability and flexibility.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a drawback of using a highly flexible workforce?
options: Lower loyalty and less knowledge of the business, which can affect service quality
Labour costs rise in periods of low demand
The business cannot respond to changes in demand
Staff cannot be moved between tasks
questions.why: Flexible workers are typically less committed, know the business less well and leave more often. In a service business, where the employee is effectively the product, that shows up in what customers experience.
whyNot: The point of flexibility is that costs FALL when demand falls.
Flexibility exists precisely to allow that response.
Multi-skilling, a form of flexibility, is about moving staff between tasks.

questions.stem: A business re-advertises a role three weeks after making it redundant. Why is this a problem?
options: It suggests the redundancy was not genuine, since the job clearly still exists
Redundant employees must be re-employed by law within a year
It proves the employee was dismissed for poor performance
Roles can never be re-advertised
questions.why: A genuine redundancy means the job has gone. Refilling it quickly indicates the job was needed, which is the clearest sign the process was actually a dismissal dressed up as a redundancy.
whyNot: There is no such general rule.
It suggests the opposite: the business wanted a different person in the same job.
Roles can be re-advertised. Doing so straight after a redundancy is what raises the question.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best definition of collective bargaining?
options: Negotiating pay and conditions for a group of employees at once, usually through a union
Each employee negotiating their own pay separately
The business setting pay with no negotiation at all
Employees buying shares in the business collectively
questions.why: One negotiation covers everybody, which is efficient for the business and gives employees real bargaining power. The cost is losing the ability to differentiate between individuals.
whyNot: That is the individual approach.
That is imposition, not bargaining.
That is employee share ownership, a different thing.

questions.stem: Why might a luxury resort treat staff as an asset while a budget airline treats them more as a cost?
options: They compete on different things: service quality against low price
Luxury businesses are legally required to pay more
Budget airlines have no employees
Asset and cost approaches are chosen at random
questions.why: What the business sells decides the approach. If customers pay for service, the staff delivering it are the product. If customers pay for the lowest fare, labour cost is a direct constraint on the price.
whyNot: There is no such legal distinction.
They employ large workforces; they manage labour cost tightly.
It is a strategic choice that follows from the business model.

questions.stem: What is the main benefit of outsourcing a function such as laundry or maintenance?
options: It converts a fixed cost into a variable one and buys in expertise
It always improves quality
It removes the need to manage the work at all
It guarantees lower total cost
questions.why: You pay for what you use rather than employing permanent staff, and the provider may be better at it. The trade-off is losing direct control of quality.
whyNot: It can reduce quality, because you no longer control how the work is done.
The contract and the provider's performance still have to be managed.
It often costs less, but not always, particularly where the provider has to travel to a remote location.

questions.stem: In a service business, why is minimising labour cost more risky than in manufacturing?
options: The employee is effectively the product, so cutting labour cuts what is being sold
Service businesses pay more tax on wages
Service businesses cannot use flexible contracts
Manufacturing has no labour costs
questions.why: In manufacturing the product exists independently of the worker who made it. In a service business the interaction IS the product, so understaffing or untrained staff directly degrade what the customer bought.
whyNot: Wage taxation does not differ by sector in that way.
Service businesses use flexible contracts heavily, particularly where demand is seasonal.
Manufacturing has substantial labour costs too.

questions.stem: A resort's demand is strongly seasonal. Which staffing approach does this most justify?
options: Seasonal contracts and multi-skilling, so capacity can scale down in the quiet season
Only permanent full-time contracts all year
Outsourcing every function including management
Reducing pay for all staff year round
questions.why: Predictable seasonal variation is exactly the case where flexibility is genuinely necessary rather than merely cheap: a fixed workforce would be idle for months.
whyNot: Permanent staff through the wet season would be paid for work that does not exist.
Core management and guest-facing roles are precisely what should not be outsourced.
A year-round pay cut addresses none of the seasonal variation and would drive staff away.

questions.stem: What is the strongest argument that a cost-minimising approach to staff can be more expensive overall?
options: High labour turnover triggers the full cost of recruiting, inducting and training again
It is illegal to pay staff the minimum wage
Cheap staff always steal from the business
Cost minimisation raises the wage bill immediately
questions.why: Every leaver restarts the recruitment and training cycle, and there is a vacancy period plus a slower learning period. Those costs are delayed and easy to overlook, which is why the approach looks cheaper than it is.
whyNot: Paying the legal minimum is lawful. The argument is economic, not legal.
An unsupported claim about people, not an argument about cost.
It lowers the immediate wage bill. The costs arrive later.
